item.title: Temi Nkem’s Oversized Braided Updo Is the Hairstyle Inspiration We Needed
item.description: Big Brother Naija 2026 winner Temi Nkem pairs a structured matte-gold leather corset and black velvet skirt with an architectural braided updo. If your next braid appointment has you thinking beyond the usual ponytail or bun, Temi Nkem has an idea you might want to take to your hairstylist. The Big Brother Naija 2026 winner wore her thick braids in a high, sculptural updo, with oversized loops arranged into a crown. She paired it with a gold-and-black look, complete with metallic beauty details and contrasting textures. Rather than letting her thick braids fall down her back, Temi has gathered them into a sleek, high updo, building them into an oversized crown of interlocking loops. The result is sculptural, full of volume and beautifully structured. It’s also a great example of how to style thick braids when you want a fresh way to wear them for an event. Pulling the hair up keeps the face open, while the loops create plenty of interest around the crown. And with the base kept sleek, the hairstyle gets to take centre stage without feeling too busy. Temi Nkem accents her sleek looped braid updo with metallic gold-leaf detailing, brow crystal, and glossy nude lips. Then there are the beauty details. Temi goes for smoky brown eyeshadow, full lashes and a glossy nude lip outlined in brown, keeping the makeup warm and complementary to the outfit. A little gold takes things further: there’s a tiny cross-shaped crystal between her brows, three vertical micro-beads on her chin, hammered circular gold earrings and flecks of metallic gold leaf tracing the side of her face, from her left temple down to her collarbone. It’s an unexpected beauty detail, and one that ties in beautifully with the colours of her outfit. Temi Nkem shows how to style thick braids into a sculptural crown paired with a gold-and-black corset gown. Now, about that gown! Temi shows how to wear gold and black with ease, starting with a structured matte-gold leather corset bodice. It features vertical seam boning, a deep V-plunge neckline and a sharply defined V-shaped basque waist. Below it, a fitted black velvet skirt brings a different texture into the look, while matching off-the-shoulder velvet arm bands complete the silhouette. The contrast between the gold leather and plush black velvet is what makes the combination work so well. Rather than having both colours compete for attention, the matte gold adds warmth and the black velvet gives the outfit balance. So, if thick braids are next on your salon mood board, you might want to save Temi’s updo. And if you’re planning a gold-and-black outfit, her mix of leather and velvet is another styling idea worth keeping. item.title: Enoch Adeagbo Was Denied Admission for Being Too Young. At 19, He’s Set to Graduate with First-Class Honours
item.description: My name is Enoch Adeagbo. In 2021, at the age of 14, I was refused admission because I was too young. I was very sad because the reason had nothing to do with my academic ability. My parents encouraged me to apply to another university, and I eventually gained admission to Ajayi Crowther University (ACU), Oyo, at the age of 14. On Wednesday, 25 November 2026, at 19, I will graduate from ACU with First Class Honours in Civil Engineering, having earned a CGPA of 4.79 out of 5.00, as the second-best student in my department and the third-best student in the Faculty of Engineering. If I had given up and not applied to another school, I might not be here today sharing my journey. Where it all began As a child, I often accompanied my father to construction sites. I enjoyed watching structures take shape from foundation stage to completion. My interest in how buildings were designed and constructed gradually developed into a desire to become an engineer. At 14, however, I was considerably younger than most of my course mates. People frequently reminded me of my age, and I had to adjust. I learnt to focus on my studies, take part in university activities and make the most of the opportunity I had been given. In the 2022/2023 session, at 15, I received the Overall Best Student in Engineering of the Year award at the 200-level. I had not expected it, but it was also an encouraging recognition of my work, and it motivated me to stay consistent. The C that taught me something But being interested in a course does not necessarily mean you’d understand it completely. I learnt this in the first semester of 400 level, when I got a C in Structural Analysis, a three-unit course I thought I understood. I was surprised because I had been confident in my knowledge of the course. That experience made me reflect on my approach to studying. I became more deliberate about understanding concepts rather than simply assuming I had mastered them. Studying with a group and teaching my coursemates also became valuable. Explaining a topic to someone else also helped me understand the course more. More than lectures Beyond the classroom, I served as the Academic Officer of the Nigerian Universities Engineering Students’ Association (NUESA), ACU Chapter, for the 2025/2026 session. I also served as an Assistant Class Representative and was involved in chapel activities as a chapel worker. My faith in God has played an important role throughout my university journey. It shaped my discipline, decisions and priorities, and helped me remain intentional about my responsibilities. I am grateful to my parents, who made sure I did not have to worry about finances while pursuing my education. Their support allowed me to concentrate on my studies and other responsibilities without the additional burden of financial concerns. item.title: Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) Joins the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts in the UK
item.description: Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) joins the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts following his Master’s degree graduation in London. Photo Credit: Debo Adedayo/Instagram Have you been keeping up with Debo Adedayo lately? Because the Nigerian actor, content creator and activist—popularly known as Mr Macaroni —just added another major feather to his cap. Debo has officially joined the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts (RSA), a UK-based institution recognised globally for bringing together changemakers across the arts, social innovation and public life. Sharing the news with his followers, Debo kept his message warm and forward-looking: I am elated to join the Fellowship of the Royal Society of Arts. Looking forward to learning, sharing and collaborating with artists from around the world who are passionate about impacting our society for good. This recognition arrives right on the heels of a busy, rewarding season for the entertainer in London. Earlier this month, Debo graduated with a Master of Arts with Distinction in Performance (Acting) from the Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts, validated by the University of East Anglia, in the United Kingdom. During his postgraduate training at Mountview, he also made his UK stage debut in July, starring as Lord Commander Thomas Fairfax in Howard Brenton’s historical play 55 Days at The Backstage Theatre in Peckham, London. Debo Adedayo brings historical figure Lord Commander Thomas Fairfax to life in James Yeatman’s stage direction of 55 Days at Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts. Photo Credit: Debo Adedayo/Instagram Long before stepping onto the London theatre stage, Debo Adedayo (born Adebowale Babatunde Adedayo ) earned his first degree in Theatre Arts and Film Studies from Redeemer’s University in 2018. Millions first came to love him in 2019 through his satirical comedy skits—creating memorable characters like Daddy Wa and Professor Hard Life—while he has steadily built an acclaimed Nollywood film career alongside his civic advocacy in Nigeria. Debo Adedayo (Mr Macaroni) holds his Master of Arts with Distinction certificate awarded by the University of East Anglia through Mountview Academy of Theatre Arts. item.title: The Design Table 2026 by So.Me Solutions: African Fashion in the Spotlight with $7,000 in Award Support for Emerging Designers
item.description: The Design Table 2026 brought together some of the voices, ideas and creative forces shaping African fashion for an afternoon of industry exchange, recognition and conversation. The annual cultural platform, produced by So.Me Solutions, welcomed designers, fashion entrepreneurs, industry leaders, media personalities and fashion enthusiasts for its latest edition. Held at GRAS Lagos, Victoria Island, during Lagos Fashion Week, this year’s gathering explored the people, perspectives and opportunities influencing the future of African fashion. The event also marked a significant milestone for So.Me Solutions, which celebrates 10 years as a 360 communications agency. Among the guests were Folake Amber (Tiffany Amber), Bola Balogun (Glam Brand), Sharon Adeleke, Beverly Naya, Awed by Moni, Marvy Olugu (House of Marvee) and Funmi Ford , alongside other familiar faces from across fashion, entertainment and the creative scene. A Seat at the Table for the Next Generation A major highlight of this year’s edition was the Next Gen Design Impact Award, which received 101 applications from emerging designers. Following the selection process, three finalists, Sultana, Dimeji Ilori and Bjuv Woman , were shortlisted for the award. The finalists were evaluated by a five-member jury comprising Dr. Yetty Ogunnubi, Odio Mimonet, Eniafe Momodu, Ugonna-Ora Owoh and Yoanna “Pepper”, with guests also participating in the voting process. Bhuv Woman emerged as the winner, receiving the $5,000 grand prize funded by Vlisco, Patrón and Culture Lab. In addition, Odio Mimonet extended a further $2,000 in award support, bringing the total prize support associated with the award to $7,000. Beyond the financial support, the winning package includes mentorship, industry access and opportunities to further advance the designer’s work. The announcement was an emotional moment for Bhuv Woman, who was visibly moved as she received the recognition and expressed gratitude to the organisers. Through the award, The Design Table continues to create opportunities for emerging designers to gain visibility, access and recognition while connecting them with established voices and resources within the fashion industry. Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion? The conversations continued with a speakers session titled “ Who Gets to Shape the Future of African Fashion?” , moderated by Yvan Otu and featured Mai Atafo , founder of ATAFO; Ezinne Chinkata , founder of Zinkata; Sacha Okoh, fashion entrepreneur and creative director of Viva; Kiki Osinbajo , founder of CIAR; and Tess Tanaka, founder of Moda54. The session explored how African fashion can move beyond being treated as a niche category and become more firmly integrated into the wider global fashion landscape. item.title: Danielle Adewusi Honours Benin Kingdom Royalty in a Self-Designed National Costume at Miss Universe 2026
item.description: Danielle Adewusi displays the sweeping circular halo backpiece and floor-length beaded train of her Benin-inspired national costume. A little Benin royalty on the Miss Universe stage? Danielle Adewusi is bringing it to Puerto Rico. For the 75th edition of the competition in San Juan, Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 has arrived at the National Costume runway with Daughter of the Coral Throne, an Edo-inspired creation that brings the history of the ancient Benin Kingdom into the spotlight. And in case you missed that detail, Danielle designed the entire look herself. Now, where do we begin with this costume? The red coral beads are everywhere, from the sheer-panelled corset bodysuit and its sweetheart neckline, trimmed with gold-toned cowrie shells, to the floor-sweeping beaded overskirt and train. Look a little closer and there’s a miniature Queen Idia mask emblem at the hip. Danielle Adewusi holds her gold ceremonial staff diagonally across Daughter of the Coral Throne against a waterside garden backdrop. Then comes the fan-shaped coral bead headpiece, followed by a sweeping circular halo backpiece with cascading bead fringes. A tall gold ceremonial staff, topped with a sculpted Queen Idia mask, completes the look. Sculpted bronze-gold motifs and thousands of beads bring the whole tribute together, with each detail drawing from the artistry and royal traditions of the Benin Kingdom. Danielle Adewusi pairs warm bronzed makeup and sleek cornrows with red coral beadwork and gold cowrie detailing. Of course, Danielle isn’t leaving us to admire the costume without knowing what inspired it. She shared the story behind Daughter of the Coral Throne, explaining how she wanted to honour her Edo heritage and celebrate a kingdom whose history and identity remain, even after many of its treasures were taken: For my Miss Universe National Costume, I honour my Edo heritage and the extraordinary legacy of the ancient Kingdom of Benin, one of Africa’s greatest civilisations… Daughter of the Coral Throne reimagines the splendour of Edo royalty through contemporary African couture. Thousands of coral-inspired beads celebrate the prestige and authority of Benin royalty, while gold detailing pays tribute to the kingdom’s master craftsmen. The circular backpiece symbolises the continuity of our ancestry, radiating across generations. In my hand, a golden ceremonial staff honours the Oba of Benin, representing leadership, royal authority and an unbroken lineage. And as I follow in my mother’s footsteps, 35 years after she wore the Miss Universe Nigeria crown, I am reminded that legacy is not simply inherited. It is preserved, honoured and carried forward. Congratulations are certainly in order for Mitchel Ukachukwu (née Ihezue )! If this is how Mitchel is introducing us to her maternity style, we’re already looking forward to more. The sweetheart neckline is gathered into a knot just above her baby bump, while the skirt falls into soft pleats, opening into a high front slit. She added a matching pleated neck scarf that flows into a long cape, with sweeping lengths of royal blue fabric suspended around her to complete the setting. Mitchel Ukachukwu marks her pregnancy reveal in a pleated royal blue gown with sweeping fabric waves. We also love how the beauty details bring everything together: chestnut-brown hair in glossy, side-parted Hollywood waves, soft bronzed makeup and understated gold jewellery. And, of course, those sweet photographs of her cradling her bump make the announcement all the more lovely. Many of us first got to know Mitchel as Mitchel Ihezue when she won the Most Beautiful Girl in Nigeria crown in 2017, before going on to claim the Miss Universe Nigeria title in 2023. Her pregnancy announcement comes nearly three years after she married Nigerian billionaire businessman and Prince Nicholas Ukachukwu , popularly known as Ikukuoma. The couple celebrated their union in December 2023 with traditional and white wedding ceremonies in Anambra State and are now preparing to welcome their first child. item.title: How to Style Green Lace for Asoebi Like Mercy Aigbe
item.description: Structural tailoring meets monochrome colour play in Mercy Aigbe’s olive and sage green asoebi look. Whenever a green dress code lands in your inbox for an upcoming wedding or celebration, the goal is always making the colour feel fresh and flattering rather than predictable. Nollywood star and filmmaker, Mercy Aigbe just gave us the sweetest blueprint for how to wear green lace for asoebi without letting heavy fabric wear you . The secret to nailing monochrome green for asoebi is mixing your shades and textures so you avoid one flat block of colour from head to toe. Mercy’s gown pairs a smooth, velvety olive corset—complete with visible boning and a central trail of beaded leaf appliqués—with a heavily beaded mermaid skirt in the same olive family . Mercy Aigbe showcases the full silhouette of her olive green corset and beaded lace mermaid gown paired with a marbled sage headtie. Keeping the bodice matte while the skirt sparkles lets the silhouette breathe, and crowning the outfit with a lighter, marbled sage headtie (gele) brightens up the face far better than a dark green wrap ever could. When taking your own green lace to the tailor, borrow her structural tricks: an asymmetrical off-the-shoulder neckline with 3D floral cutouts draws the eye upward, while a diagonal beaded sash-peplum along one hip creates curves without adding bulk around your waist. Mercy Aigbe pairs her olive green lace outfit with a deep red crystal crescent clutch and matching red manicure. As for how to accessorise a green monochrome outfit, skip the usual all-gold default and bring in a rich contrast colour. Olive and sage sit right opposite red on the colour wheel, which is why Mercy’s gold jewellery set with dark red stones, crescent red crystal clutch, and glossy red nails pop so well against the green . Paired with warm golden-bronze eyeshadow and a glossy nude-brown lip , the whole look feels balanced, celebratory, and ready for any guest list. item.title: Ghana’s Black Challenge Conquer the World With First-Ever Amputee Football World Cup Title
item.description: Pure joy on the pitch as Ghana’s Black Challenge mark their historic 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup triumph in Mexico. Ghana’s national amputee football team, the Black Challenge, have officially conquered the world after edging Morocco 1–0 in the final of the 2026 World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF) World Cup in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico on Sunday, November 22, 2026. For anyone keeping an eye on international football and West African sporting milestones, this is a moment worth celebrating—it marks Ghana’s very first Amputee Football World Cup crown. The championship match brought together two African powerhouses and served as a high-stakes showdown between familiar rivals, following Ghana’s earlier continental triumphs against Morocco, including the 2024 African Amputee Cup of Nations final. Captain Richard Arthur Opentil stepped up as the decisive hero, scoring the lone goal in the 32nd minute. From there, Ghana dug deep with grit, smart positioning, and defensive discipline to shut out Morocco and bring the trophy home. Intense action between Morocco and Ghana during the 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup in Mexico. What makes Ghana’s run in Mexico even more memorable is how much they had to overcome in the knockout stages. The Black Challenge defeated the United States 3–1 in the Round of 16, eased past Egypt 2–0 in the quarter-finals behind a brace from forward Mubarik Mohammed , and then edged a tense semi-final 1–1 after extra time before winning 4–3 on penalties. Individual brilliance shone right alongside the team trophy. Forward Mubarik Mohammed finished as the tournament’s top scorer with seven goals, earning the Golden Boot award. Back home, the achievement sparked widespread celebration, with congratulatory messages from Ghana’s leadership—including President John Dramani Mahama and the Ministry of Sports and Recreation—alongside financial backing and pledges from corporate supporters and philanthropists such as Gold Fields Ghana and Mohammed Raii through the EEZZY Group Foundation. Speaking after the victory, captain Richard Arthur Opentil dedicated the triumph to Ghana and its supporters as an early Christmas gift to the nation. Ghana’s Black Challenge celebrate lifting their maiden 2026 WAFF Amputee Football World Cup trophy in San Juan de los Lagos, Mexico. If you are wondering what the WAFF Amputee Football World Cup is all about, it is the premier international championship for amputee football, governed globally by the World Amputee Football Federation (WAFF). Played according to rules adapted from FIFA’s Laws of the Game, amputee football is fast-paced, physically demanding, and thrilling to watch. Matches feature seven players per side—outfield players with lower-limb amputations playing on forearm crutches without prostheses, and goalkeepers with single-arm amputations—with crutches treated as part of the player’s body rather than a tool to intentionally play the ball. item.title: From Mind Games to Ghost Stories! 5 Nollywood Titles to Stream This Week
item.description: Wande Thomas’s psychological thriller Spiraling, starring Toni Tones, Jim Iyke, Folu Storms and Seun Ajayi on KAVA, is among the titles recommended to watch this week. Wrongfully accused, caught in a web of lies, pulled into a dangerous family feud or haunted by a past you never saw coming. This week’s streaming picks have a little bit of everything for anyone who enjoys a story that refuses to let them relax. We’ve rounded up five titles across Circuits, Netflix, Prime Video and KAVA, taking you from psychological thrillers and gang conflicts to supernatural mysteries and a night out that spirals into something much bigger. Extra Mile — Circuits Sometimes trying to do a good deed for someone else is how everything goes sideways. That is the trap at the heart of this drama, where a woman ends up behind bars for a crime she never committed after stepping in to help a friend. Mercy Johnson – Okojie , Jim Iyke and Lilian Esoro carry the story forward under Kayode Kasum ‘s direction, working from a screenplay by Folasade Osibo and with Joy Grant – Ekong and Solate Ovundah – Akarolo on board as producers. Double Decoy — Circuits Moving from courtroom-style heartbreak straight into psychological mind games, our next pick on the same platform turns suspicion into a sport. Nothing looks straightforward when hidden agendas, shifting loyalties and high-stakes deception collide in this tense thriller. As every move feels like a test of trust, viewers are left guessing who is really pulling the strings, anchored by Kanayo O . Kanayo , Sola Sobowale and Gideon Okeke . Behind the scenes, the credits point to Oluwafemi Isaac Akinsipe alongside Nnamdi E . Odunze and Chichi Stylxz . The Covenant Season 2 — Netflix If that kind of high-stakes tension gets you in the mood for bigger battles and family rivalries, head over to Netflix next where the stakes climb even higher. item.title: Solape Fayemi Launches Saina Properties Across Four Markets
item.description: For many people, buying property is one of the biggest financial decisions they will ever make. Yet, knowing who to trust, how to verify ownership and whether a property is worth the investment can make the process overwhelming. It is a challenge Solape Fayemi hopes to address with the launch of Saina Properties , a real estate company now operating across Nigeria, the United Kingdom, the United States and the United Arab Emirates. Officially unveiled at an event held on 17 November at the Marriott Hotel, Ikeja GRA, Lagos, Saina Properties is built around a simple idea: property ownership should be guided by sound advice, proper verification and professional support, not just the excitement of closing a deal. For Solape, whose experience in the investment industry shaped her understanding of money, risk and wealth creation, the decision to establish the company came from recognising the need for a more considered approach to real estate. “We are not building Saina Properties because the world needs another company selling properties. We are building Saina because we believe there is room for a different kind of real estate experience. One where advice comes before the transaction, where due diligence is not treated as an inconvenience, and where people are encouraged to ask questions, understand their options and make informed decisions,” she said at the launch. That philosophy is reflected in the company’s three core areas of expertise: Advisory & Verification, Sales & Brokerage, and Developments . Rather than focusing solely on connecting buyers to properties, Saina brings together the guidance investors need to assess opportunities, the support required to navigate property transactions, and involvement in real estate development. The company is also building on experience gained before its official launch, having supported more than 25 clients with property opportunities across different markets. An important part of its proposition is the role of professional expertise in protecting property investors. Fayemi’s position raises a familiar question: people consult doctors for medical concerns and lawyers for legal matters, so why do some investors leave significant property decisions in the hands of relatives simply because they are available or familiar with the location? I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha! One thing about me is that I like to be involved. item.description: Have you ever spent six hours in an airport waiting for your connecting flight, watching the departure screens, browsing duty-free shops and wondering what the city outside looks like? Perhaps you were connecting through Istanbul, Doha, Dubai or Addis Ababa. You were technically in another country, but the closest you came to experiencing it was buying a souvenir at the airport. What if I told you that some airlines could help you turn that connection into an additional holiday, sometimes even providing accommodation? Having travelled to more than 70 countries, I have learnt that one of the smartest ways to travel is to pay attention to the journey, not just the destination. Many Nigerians book international tickets based on price, travel time and baggage allowance. These are important considerations, but there is another question worth asking: What else can this ticket give me? I am talking about stopovers, not the hurried two-hour connection where you are running between terminals, but an intentional break in your journey that allows you to experience another destination before continuing to the country you originally planned to visit. And with the right airline, itinerary and travel documents, that additional experience might cost less than you imagine. For example, imagine travelling from Lagos to London through Istanbul. Instead of spending a few hours at Istanbul Airport, you could investigate whether your ticket qualifies for a longer stopover, allowing you to explore Istanbul before continuing to London. You have now turned one international journey into an opportunity to experience two destinations outside Nigeria. The secret is to investigate the stopover before purchasing your ticket, rather than arriving at the airport and hoping the airline will allow you to stay longer. item.title: Beyond the Mini LED Label: What Should Define Good Mini LED Performance?
item.description: The presence of Mini LED tells a shopper something important about the light source behind an LCD panel. It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? Where TCL Enters The Category Conversation TCL is relevant to that discussion because Mini LED has become a significant part of its global television business. According to Omdia data cited in TCL Electronics interim results, TCL ranked No. 1 globally by Mini LED TV shipment volume in the first half of 2026. TCL reported 2.43 million Mini LED TV shipments during the period, representing 77.1% year on year growth. That position follows a strong 2025, when TCL reported, based on Omdia data, a 31.1% share of global Mini LED TV shipments and 118.0% year on year shipment growth. item.title: A Safari, a Beach & Easy Entry? 5 African Spots for Your Christmas Holiday
item.description: Five African destinations Nigerian passport holders can visit visa-free or with visa on arrival this Christmas holiday. Image: AI-generated. The group chat has the concerts, the dinners and the Detty December link-ups covered. But has anyone planned the getaway? Beyond the usual Lagos parties and end-of-year outings, there is a whole continent waiting to be explored, with sun-soaked beaches, wildlife safaris, exciting food scenes and cities with plenty of stories to tell. You do not have to spend weeks navigating embassy appointments and visa applications to make it happen, either. Several African countries offer Nigerian passport holders visa-free entry or visas on arrival, making a festive-season escape much easier to plan. Whether you are travelling solo, gathering your friends, taking the family along or joining a curated travel group, here are five destinations worth considering for your Christmas holiday. Kenya Imagine spotting lions and giraffes against a city skyline before breakfast, then catching an evening flight or train straight to the coast for fresh seafood by the Indian Ocean. That contrast is what makes Kenya such a rewarding December escape. Nairobi gives you immediate access to wildlife at Nairobi National Park and the Giraffe Centre alongside lively restaurants and art spaces in Westlands and Karen, while longer itineraries open up classic game drives in the Maasai Mara, views of Mount Kilimanjaro in Amboseli, and warm beach days in Diani or Watamu. Nigerian citizens enjoy visa-free entry for short stays of up to 60 days without needing a paid eTA, leaving more room in your budget for safaris and coastal stays. Rwanda Not everyone wants their year-end holiday to feel like a non-stop sprint, and Rwanda is built for travellers who prefer scenery, clean air, and an unhurried pace. From the capital, you can track chimpanzees and walk above the trees in Nyungwe Forest, go on wildlife drives in Akagera National Park, or spend quiet afternoons along the shores of Lake Kivu. With 30-day visa-free entry for Nigerian passport holders, getting there is straightforward from start to finish. item.description: From music visuals to international festival stages and actor-turned-director debuts, Dammy Twitch, Akinola Davies Jr., and Daniel Etim Effiong represent different paths into Nollywood directing. Think about the Nigerian films and series you have watched recently, the ones that kept you glued to your screen, had you talking about the storyline long after the credits rolled or recommending them to everyone you know. While the actors are often the faces you remember first, there is someone behind the camera whose creative choices help bring those stories to life: the director. From interpreting the script and guiding actors to shaping how each scene looks, sounds and unfolds, directors influence almost every part of what ends up on screen. As Nollywood grows in ambition, production quality and global reach, the filmmakers steering these projects are becoming just as central to the industry’s story as the stars in front of the lens. Some have spent decades bringing Nigerian literature and history to the screen, while others are earning international acclaim or crossing over from music videos into feature films. Here are five Nollywood directors whose work is worth knowing. Tunde Kelani Start with Tunde Kelani if you want to see where modern Nigerian cinema found its literary and cultural roots. Trained at the London Film School after cutting his teeth in photography and television, the Mainframe Films founder has spent decades turning Nigerian literature, stage plays, and history into lasting screen works. Titles like Ti Oluwa Nile , Koseegbe , O Le Ku , Saworoide , Thunderbolt: Magun , The Narrow Path , Maami , Dazzling Mirage , Ayinla , and Cordelia show how wide his range goes. Across years of festivals and awards, Kelani has collected major honours for his craft, and his adaptation Cordelia earned him a Best Director nomination at the 2026 Africa Magic Viewers’ Choice Awards. Tunde Kelani, whose directing catalogue spans Ti Oluwa Nile, Saworoide, The Narrow Path, Maami, and Cordelia, with Kunle Afolayan outdoors. Photo Credit: Tunde Kelani/Instagram Akinola Davies Jr. Few directors have linked global festival stages with homegrown Nollywood triumphs quite like Akinola Davies Jr. After his short film Lizard won the Short Film Grand Jury Prize at the Sundance Film Festival in 2021, he co-wrote and directed his feature debut My Father’s Shadow alongside his brother Wale Davies . The drama made history in 2025 as the first Nigerian film selected for the Official Selection at the Cannes Film Festival, picking up a Special Mention for the Caméra d’Or before winning Best Director at the British Independent Film Awards and Breakthrough Director at the Gotham Independent Film Awards. His momentum rolled straight into 2026 with a BAFTA win for Outstanding Debut by a British Writer, Director or Producer, followed by Best Director and Best Overall Movie wins at the 2026 AMVCAs. item.title: Esther Adeyanju: This International Men’s Day, Let’s Make Room for Men’s Vulnerability
item.description: “Men are not wired to show emotions.” A male friend once said to me during an argument. He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Frequent questions men are asked: “How far? Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. Society has an interesting checklist for measuring a man’s success. A good job, a house, a car, a wife, children and financial stability. Preferably, all achieved before a certain age. But if a man struggles to achieve all these, is his life any less meaningful? Surely, a man’s worth cannot be reduced to his bank balance, job title or ability to convince everyone that he has everything under control. There must be room for men who are still becoming. item.title: Burna Boy, Asake & Seyi Vibez Bring Afrobeats to the World of GTA VI
item.description: From left: Nigerian artists Asake, Seyi Vibez, and Burna Boy, whose songs appear in Grand Theft Auto VI. How else could Grand Theft Auto VI begin than with Nigerian artists featured in the music lineup of the biggest video game release of the year? As players around the world finally step into Rockstar Games’ highly anticipated open-world action-adventure title, Burna Boy , Asake , and Seyi Vibez are making sure Nigerian music is front and centre on the virtual streets of Vice City and the wider state of Leonida. Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI) officially arrives today, Thursday, 19 November 2026, on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S, ending a 13-year wait since Grand Theft Auto V first hit consoles. Developed and published by Rockstar Games, the open-world action-adventure game follows dual protagonists Jason and Lucia across the sun-soaked, neon-lit state of Leonida—a fictional take on Florida that brings players back to Vice City in the franchise’s largest map yet. Music has always been at the heart of the Grand Theft Auto universe, where players tune into curated in-game radio stations while driving or walking around town, and this sixth instalment takes African soundscapes seriously. At the centre of the Nigerian presence is AfroBank FM, a dedicated African music radio station inside Grand Theft Auto VI that is co-hosted by Grammy winner Burna Boy—credited on-air simply as Burna—alongside British DJ and producer Palms Trax , who goes by Palmsy. Curated to spotlight everything from 20th-century African classics to contemporary Afrobeats, amapiano, and 3-step, the station features Asake’s 2022 hit “ Joha ” from his debut album Mr Money With The Vibe , as well as “ Giza “, the 2023 collaboration between Burna Boy and Seyi Vibez from Burna Boy’s seventh studio album I Told Them …. Alongside those tracks, Burna Boy also appears on the game’s official companion soundtrack album, Grand Theft Auto VI: The Album, with his original song “ Bigger ” sitting on a 34-track roster that includes Travis Scott , Cardi B , Dua Lipa , SZA , Tame Impala , and Lana Del Rey . The African representation on AfroBank FM stretches beyond Nigeria too, sharing airwaves with Ghanaian highlife legends Pat Thomas and Ebo Taylor on “ Gye Wani ” and South African stars DJ Lag , Robot Boii , and Kamo Mphela on “ Shay’sana “. With players able to listen to Leonida’s terrestrial radio stations both in vehicles and on foot through in-game headphones, millions of gamers worldwide are now cruising through Vice City with Burna Boy on the mic and Asake and Seyi Vibez on heavy rotation. item.title: How La Roche-Posay Brought Skin Science to Over 500 Guests in Its First Living Lab Experience
item.description: La Roche-Posay concluded its first Living Lab experience in Nigeria, welcoming Nigerian stakeholders to its opening party and three-day programme, held from 4 to 6 November 2026 at Oasis by The Five Palm, Victoria Island, Lagos. Inspired by the original Living Lab concept in Paris, the experience brought the science, research and expertise behind skincare closer to Nigerian consumers and healthcare professionals. It marked the brand’s first Living Lab in the country, creating a platform for more accessible conversations around skin health, dermatological innovation and everyday skincare. The experience opened with an exclusive session for healthcare professionals and invited guests before welcoming members of the public over the following two days. Each day featured three expert-led sessions exploring the role of dermatology and scientific research in advancing skin health, the wider impact of skin conditions on everyday life, and the importance of understanding product safety, tolerance and efficacy. The sessions brought together healthcare professionals and representatives from across Nigeria’s dermatological beauty and skincare community, encouraging knowledge-sharing and stronger connections between science, expertise and consumer education. Visitors explored five dedicated Innovation Corners showcasing La Roche-Posay’s Effaclar, Mela B3, Anthelios, Cicaplast and Lipikar ranges. Each space introduced visitors to specific skin concerns and the science behind the brand’s product formulations. Through interactive demonstrations and guided product experiences, guests gained a better understanding of different skin concerns and the role of targeted skincare in addressing them. At the Anthelios corner, visitors used a UV camera to see the effects of ultraviolet exposure and better understand the importance of sun protection. The Effaclar and Mela B3 spaces explored concerns including blemishes and hyperpigmentation, while the Cicaplast and Lipikar corners introduced visitors to approaches to caring for sensitive, damaged and dry skin. Beyond the Innovation Corners, visitors explored the Blue House, which presented La Roche-Posay’s history and commitment to dermatological innovation, and the Scars of Life Cinema. The cinema screened a 25-minute film exploring the physical and psychological realities of living with scars and scarring, including their impact on self-image and everyday life. The film also highlighted how Lipikar supports the care of skin affected by scarring, bringing attention to the importance of addressing both the visible and less visible experiences associated with skin conditions. The programme also created opportunities for visitors to engage with skincare experts and dermatologists through one-on-one consultations, ask questions about their individual skin concerns and receive guidance on building appropriate skincare routines. Bringing different voices, personalities and perspectives to the proceedings, the line-up reflected the reach of an awards platform whose story has grown alongside the generations of young Africans it recognises. The hosts also shared the spotlight with Infinity , an AI assistant that introduced another dimension to the evening. item.title: International Men’s Day: Six Films That Explore the Vulnerable Side of Men
item.description: One of the best aspects of art is its ability to imitate current events or imagine possibilities. Movies, as a powerful art form, present a sequence of events that allows viewers to see reflections of themselves or envision who they could become. At its core, art exists to entertain, inform and critique society. Through films, music and visual expressions, we are continually reminded of our shared humanity—our joys, flaws and contradictions. One subject that art, particularly film, has explored is masculinity. However, this theme is often addressed subtly and can be easy to overlook, as the movies that dominate global box offices frequently focus on spectacle: fantasy, romance, adventure or others. Conversations about men, their inner lives, vulnerabilities and social roles are often not in the top circle. Nonetheless, some films have attempted to explore what it means to be a man in today’s world. They invite audiences to contemplate important questions such as: What is the role of men in society? What defines a man? How does a man’s behaviour influence those around him? What expectations does society place on men? What responsibilities do men have within society? Where does responsibility begin, and where does it end? Do men matter? Do their feelings matter? The theme for this year’s International Men’s Day is “The Future Is For Everyone.” For that, here are some movies that explore and illuminate the complexities of masculinity: The Pursuit of Happyness This classic film reveals the vulnerability often hidden behind male perseverance. Will Smith ’s portrayal of Chris Gardner challenges the stoic notion of manhood by showing fatherhood as both an act of love and endurance. Through his struggles with homelessness, rejection, and exhaustion, the film redefines masculinity, depicting it as the courage to remain tender even when life tests your strength in every way. Fatherhood Kevin Hart ’s film Fatherhood delves into themes of grief and single parenthood, balancing humour with heartfelt moments. It challenges traditional expectations of masculinity by illustrating a father’s journey through uncertainty, learning empathy, and committing to being present for his child/ren. Through this film, Kevin Hart shares his vision of what it means to be a man and a father. Adolescence Adolescence examines how boys internalise distorted notions of strength and freedom, and how escaping them demands emotional awareness. The film reveals the journey of a young boy on the brink of adulthood, revealing the pressures of identity and self-definition. item.title: Tunji Olowolafe Wants Ikogosi to Be Nigeria’s Next Destination for Weddings, Retreats and Landmark Celebrations
item.description: Growing up, Tunji Olowolafe ’s parents brought the family to Are-Ekiti every Christmas, and a trip to Ikogosi was compulsory. Decades later, he returned to the warm springs town with family, friends and business partners, “not to take away, but to help build something enduring in Ekiti.” Speaking as Chairman and Chief Launcher of Ikogosi Day 2026, Thanksgiving and Launch of the Oba’s Palace Project, on Saturday, 14 November 2026, the Chancellor of Ekiti State University set out a vision for Ikogosi built on intentional tourism, enterprise and heritage. Dr. Olowolafe said Ikogosi’s task now is to give visitors compelling reasons to come, stay longer and spend across local businesses. He pointed to the recent Ikogosi 17.5km Race, which drew runners from across Nigeria alongside athletes from Ghana, Kenya and Ethiopia, as an example of what happens when private initiative meets local hospitality. He urged the same thinking for lifestyle and executive tourism, with the ambition of making Ikogosi a premier international destination for weddings, milestone birthdays, corporate retreats and landmark gatherings. “Our natural landscape will draw people in. But only the quality of the experience we deliver, through warmth of welcome, impeccable service and attention to detail, will bring them back,” he said. To build that service culture, he called for a deeper, structured partnership between the Ikogosi Resort and the Hospitality Management Technology Department of the Federal Polytechnic, Ado-Ekiti, which has already produced two sets of National Diploma graduates. The goal is for students to train alongside seasoned professionals while serving real guests. He also proposed alliances with leading international hospitality institutes to benchmark local teaching and service, noting that world-class hospitality must become Ekiti’s signature. He argued that the same commercial discipline must apply to the resources beneath the ground. “It is not enough to say we have clay or kaolin. We must ask: What are their exact industrial specifications? What can we competitively manufacture? And who is ready to buy?” he said. He tasked the Department of Geology at Ekiti State University, headed by Professor Yinka Aturamu , with establishing precise data on local deposits and mapping out what it would take to turn them into viable commercial enterprises. For him, the measure of success is what it changes for young people in the community. “For a young person growing up in Ikogosi, the result must be tangible: a marketable skill, a steady job, a supply contract or a thriving enterprise,” he said. He cited Rasheed Sarumi’s Saroafrica Group as proof of what is possible. The group acquired Gossy Warm Springs in 2018 and restored the plant to full production in 2019. Together with its partners, Saroafrica is now investing US$25 million in a manufacturing facility in Ikogosi, which will run on its own 2MW gas-fired power plant. item.title: Miss Universe 2026: Meet the 17 African Queens Representing the Continent
item.description: From left: Miss Universe Democratic Republic of the Congo 2026 Jessi Kalambayi, Miss Universe Namibia 2026 Charene Labuschagne, and Miss Universe Botswana 2026 Dabilo Moses ahead of the 75th Miss Universe finale in San Juan, Puerto Rico. The Miss Universe stage is getting a beautiful dose of African representation this year, with 17 contestants from across the continent making their way to Puerto Rico for the pageant’s 75th edition. And there are plenty of stories to discover among them, from Uganda ’s historic debut to Nigeria ’s Danielle Adewusi , whose journey to the competition comes with a lovely family connection. Taking place in San Juan, Puerto Rico, the Diamond Anniversary edition will bring together 116 contestants from around the world, all hoping to claim the newly unveiled 75th-anniversary crown, The Radiance of an Eternal Legacy. The grand finale is scheduled for Tuesday, 24 November 2026, at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum. This year’s show will be hosted by R’Bonney Gabriel , Mario Lopez , Zuri Hall and Dayanara Torres . At the end of the night, reigning Miss Universe 2025 Fátima Bosch of Mexico will pass on her crown to a new winner. Bosch took the title in Thailand last November, ahead of contestants from Thailand, Venezuela, the Philippines and Côte d’Ivoire. For Africa, the road to this year’s competition has come with a few changes. Angola, the Republic of the Congo, South Sudan, Zambia and Zimbabwe were unable to participate due to U.S. travel and visa restrictions, while Côte d’Ivoire, Mauritius, Rwanda and Senegal withdrew from the competition. Still, 17 African countries have contestants in the running, including Uganda, which is making its historic Miss Universe debut. Cameroon, Ethiopia, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Tunisia are among the countries returning to the global stage. Representing Nigeria is 29-year-old medical doctor and women’s health advocate Danielle Adewusi, also known as Danielle Fadeke Adewusi. Her participation adds a special family detail to the story: she won Miss Universe Nigeria 2026 in Lagos, 35 years after her mother, Tonia Okogbenin , represented the country at Miss Universe 1991. From first-time participation to familiar faces returning to the competition, these are the 17 African beauty queens representing the continent at Miss Universe 2026. Dabilo Moses — Botswana Representing Botswana is 26-year-old Dabilo Moses from Gaborone (born in Tutume). A Broadcasting and Journalism student at Limkokwing University of Creative Technology, she previously won Miss Independence Botswana 2022, reached the Top 24 at Miss Supranational 2023 as Botswana’s first-ever entrant, and was appointed Miss Universe Botswana 2026 after finishing as first runner-up in 2025. item.description: The evolving business of content creation took centre stage in Lagos as Woof Studios Africa , in partnership with Insight Redefini , hosted the second edition of PluggedIN 2026 in Victoria Island, Lagos. The gathering brought together some of Nigeria’s leading content creators, filmmakers, advertising professionals and brand executives to explore how digital influence can translate into original intellectual property, sustainable creative businesses and longer-term commercial opportunities. Hosted by actress and media personality Bisola Aiyeola , the event gave creators a platform to present original concepts and explore new possibilities for collaboration with brands and industry stakeholders. From Content Creation to Intellectual Property A major highlight of PluggedIN 2026 was its creator showcase, featuring Taaooma, Layi Wasabi, Aproko Doctor, Ify’s Kitchen, Biodun Stephen, Osas Ighodaro, Shank Comics, Folagade Banks, Afropolitan, Bolaji Ogunmola, and Geena Foodies n Spice . The creators presented original ideas, show formats and potential collaborative projects, offering a glimpse into the range of stories and formats emerging from Nigeria’s creative community. The opportunity for brands lies in being part of that process through partnerships that go beyond individual sponsored posts to support the development, production and distribution of original content. For Adetutu Laditan , Creator Economy Catalyst and Founder of Woof Studios Africa, this shift requires a more structured approach to supporting creators and connecting them with the right opportunities. “Our vision at Woof Studios Africa has always been to empower African creators to move beyond virality and build lasting, profitable enterprises. Nigerian creators are thinking bigger, and forward-thinking brands want to be part of that evolution,” she said. Laditan explained that Woof Studios works across the business and production aspects of content development, including funding and distribution, to help creators take ideas beyond their initial digital formats. “When creators understand a brand’s business objectives, and brands respect the authentic voice a creator has spent years cultivating, we stop simply buying attention and start co-creating stories that matter.” The conversations at PluggedIN also addressed the realities of building sustainable creative businesses. During the creator-focused panel, Kiekie, Craze Clown, Jay On-Air and Winifred Nwania of Zeelicious Food discussed the opportunities and challenges of building careers in the digital space. They explored content ownership, audience engagement, monetisation and the importance of meaningful brand relationships. item.title: Ibukun Awosika, Juliet Ibrahim, Bola Adesola & More: Leading Women Take Centre Stage at The Executive Woman Summit 2.0
item.description: What does it really mean to play to win in business and leadership? Beyond earning a seat at the table, it requires more than competence or professional accomplishments. It requires the confidence to own one’s value, the clarity to communicate one’s contributions and the intentionality to build visibility that translates into meaningful influence. These conversations defined The Executive Woman Summit (TEWS) 2.0 , which brought together hundreds of executive women, corporate professionals, entrepreneurs and emerging leaders at Harbour Point, Victoria Island, Lagos, on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Convened by Bola Matel-Okoh , a dual-qualified attorney (called to both the New York and Nigerian Bars), Executive Coach, Non-Executive Director at Wema Bank, and CEO of BMO Advisory Services , the second edition of the summit was themed Playing to Win: Elevate Your Vision, Value and Visibility. It provided an intentional platform for candid conversations, practical insights and strategic alliances on what it takes for women to advance, lead and thrive in today’s evolving corporate landscape. In her opening address, Matel-Okoh challenged women to rethink how they approach professional visibility, authority and advancement. According to her, competence is merely the baseline; it is not enough if you are unwilling to communicate your value, own your voice and position yourself for higher-stakes opportunities. This philosophy also came through in her cover interview with THISDAY Glitterati ahead of the summit, where she offered a compelling perspective on the distinction between holding a powerful position and exercising genuine influence. “A powerful position gives you formal authority. Influence determines how deeply your leadership shapes people’s thinking, decisions and actions. A title may secure your place in a meeting, but credibility makes people listen,” she explained. She also challenged the assumption that excellent work will automatically speak for itself, encouraging women to communicate their contributions with evidence and confidence. “What problem did you solve? What result did you produce? What changed because of your leadership?” she asked, highlighting the importance of making professional value visible to the decision-makers who influence career progression and boardroom opportunities. “There is no need to diminish your achievements to make others comfortable. You can be gracious and still be clear about the value you bring,” she added. The summit featured a distinguished line-up of women shaping leadership, business, finance, entertainment and corporate governance. Chairman of Ecobank Nigeria, Bola Adesola , and CEO of FS Global Advisory Services, Folake Sanu , delivered keynote addresses, sharing perspectives on leadership, professional growth, boardroom dynamics and navigating the demands of executive life. item.title: Inside the 2026 WIEN Gala & Awards: A Night of Celebration, Powerful Conversations and a New DEI Benchmark
item.description: The Metropolitan Club, Lagos, was transformed into a gathering of some of the most influential names in Nigeria’s energy industry as the Women in Energy Network (WIEN) hosted its 2026 Gala & Awards. Bringing together industry leaders, policymakers, corporate executives and other distinguished guests, the evening marked six years of WIEN’s advocacy for greater representation, inclusion and leadership opportunities for women across the energy value chain. Beyond the glamour, elegant conversations and celebrations, the event carried a clear message: it is time to move beyond conversations about inclusion and focus on measurable progress. The Honourable Minister of Women Affairs and Social Development, Hajia Imaan Sulaiman-Ibrahim , delivered the special address, ably represented by Dr Adedayo Benjamins-Laniyi , Director-General/Chief Executive Officer of the Maryam Babangida National Centre for Women Development . In her address, WIEN President Eyono Fatayi-Williams emphasised that progress must be visible, measurable and sustained. “As we celebrate six years, we also have to ask ourselves an important question: What do the next six years look like? Because we cannot spend the next six years having the same conversations we have had in the last six years. We cannot continue to talk about inclusion without asking what has changed,” Fatayi-Williams challenged the industry. The evening also featured a keynote address by Dr Mutiu Sunmonu (CON) , Chairman of The Sage Centre for Leadership Excellence, who shared perspectives on leadership and the importance of creating opportunities for women to contribute meaningfully to the sector. Six Years of Building Opportunities for Women Reflecting on the organisation’s growth and the realities of navigating the energy sector, WIEN Board of Trustees Chairperson, Dr Cecilia Aqua Umoren , challenged guests to strive for true parity. “In the six years that WIEN has been in existence, we have created more opportunities for women, resulting in numerous appointments and an expanded STEM pipeline. However, progress is not parity; we are ultimately aiming for true parity. We must acknowledge that most leadership positions today are occupied by men, meaning we cannot achieve our objectives without partnering with them to create access. If the room is not created for you, create your own room, set your own table, and be at your own table.” WIEN’s Executive Secretary, Asanimo Omezi , echoed this commitment, highlighting the network’s growth from a collective of 30 women to more than 1,000 members, supported by 30 corporate partners. “We started as a small collective of just 30 women, and today we have grown to over a thousand members with thirty corporate partners. They want solutions that are intuitive, efficient and capable of making daily life easier. item.description: Beyoncé becomes the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram If you have ever wondered what triple digits look like on music’s biggest stage, Beyoncé just gave everyone the answer. The Houston-born global music superstar has officially become the first artist in history to reach 100 career Grammy nominations, hitting the milestone with her latest nod for “ Morning Dew ( Donk )”, which is nominated for Best R&B Solo Performance at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards (2027 Grammys). Released in July 2026 ahead of the 20th anniversary of her sophomore album B’Day, “Morning Dew (Donk)” puts her in a category alongside Kehlani , Victoria Monét , Jill Scott , and Nigerian star Tems . To put the 100-nomination milestone into perspective, no other recording artist has ever crossed into triple digits since the Grammys began. Beyoncé had previously been tied with her husband, Jay-Z , at 88 nominations each before breaking that tie in 2024 with 11 nods for Cowboy Carter to reach 99—and this latest recognition pushes her even further ahead as the artist with the highest number of Grammy nominations in history. Beyoncé holding her three Grammy trophies at the 67th Annual Grammy Awards in 2025. Photo Credit: Beyoncé/Instagram It is also a good reminder of how long she has been doing this at the highest level. Beyoncé’s Grammy journey started all the way back in 2000 as part of Destiny’s Child with “Bills, Bills, Bills”, and across more than two decades as a solo artist, group member, and collaborator, she has built a record that keeps stretching further ahead of the pack. Alongside holding the title for the most Grammy nominations of all time, she is already the most awarded artist in Grammy history with 35 wins, a record she first broke in 2023 when she surpassed late conductor Georg Solti ’s 31 trophies. She pushed that tally even higher at the 2025 Grammys, taking home three awards—Album of the Year and Best Country Album for Cowboy Carter, as well as Best Country Duo/Group Performance for “II Most Wanted” alongside Miley Cyrus . Now all eyes turn to Sunday, 7 February 2027, when the 2027 Grammy Awards take place at the Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles and we find out whether nomination number 100 turns into Grammy win number 36. item.title: Tochukwu Ekoh: What My Friend’s Passing Taught Me About Kindness
item.description: A thoughtful young woman sits in a relaxed pose in a serene bedroom, reflecting peacefully. Photo credit: Alex Green/Pexels. I lost someone recently, and since then, I have found myself revisiting little moments, conversations and encounters I probably would not have given much thought to otherwise. We weren’t particularly close , or I wouldn’t describe our relationship that way . We had reconnected after a long time and started seeing each other more often, especially after I resumed work following an accident I was involved in. He gradually became part of my daily routine. Whenever I went to work, he would come to pick me up from the office, and we would go home together. In many ways, he looked out for me and made sure I got home safely. We started talking more. We would discuss life, share experiences and occasionally open up about things happening in our individual lives. There was also an emotional dimension to our friendship. He was interested in me romantically, I realised, but I didn’t feel the same way. I tried to understand my feelings, but the truth was that I simply wasn’t in love with him. I couldn’t manufacture feelings that weren’t there. Then I heard that he passed away. My first reaction, strangely, was guilt. I began asking myself: Was I a good friend to him? Was I kind enough? Was I considerate? Did I treat him well? Could I have done something differently? I caught myself wondering whether I should have given him a chance . Perhaps I should have allowed him to love me. But then would I have done that out of genuine affection or simply out of pity? And would that have been fair to either of us? My understanding is that not returning someone’s romantic feelings does not mean we cannot offer them genuine friendship, kindness and compassion. I didn’t owe him romantic love, but I could have been a good friend. That has stayed with me. Beyond the guilt, there was another question I couldn’t get out of my head: Why did God allow us to reconnect? Why, after such a long time, did our paths have to cross again? Why did we have to start talking, sharing experiences and becoming familiar with each other again, only for him to die shortly afterwards? Why him? Why at that particular time? What was the reason for that reconnection, and why did it have to end this way? The timing of certain events leaves you with more questions than answers. item.title: Entertainment Week Africa officially kicks Off 5th Edition in Lagos | November 17th – 22nd
item.description: Entertainment Week Africa (EWA) , the pan-African platform for the business of creativity, opens its fifth edition in Lagos tomorrow, Wednesday, 18 November. The programme runs until Saturday, 21 November, and brings together creators, executives, investors, policymakers and delegations from more than 18 African countries. This year’s theme, Five Years of Closing the Gap, reflects the purpose EWA was built around: connecting African talent with the capital, markets, skills and audiences it needs to grow. Since its first edition, EWA has welcomed more than 67,800 attendees. The 2025 edition alone recorded 28,683 pass-holders from over eight countries and 50 industries, across 61 sessions, 93 film screenings, 20 music showcases and nine fashion showcases. By day and by night The week runs across two venues. By day, EbonyLife Place on Victoria Island hosts panels, roundtables, workshops, masterclasses, and film screenings. By night, the programme moves to the Livespot Entertarium in Ikate, beginning with Opening Night on 18 November at 6pm, an evening of music, fashion, film, comedy and awards. The Entertarium also houses the week’s experiences, including an exhibition, the EWA Art Floor, a fashion show, comedy, live music, a beauty exhibition and a marketplace. Seven tracks, one market The 2026 programme is organised across seven tracks: Film & TV; Music; Fashion & Beauty; AI & Tech; Live Events & Production; Creative Enterprise; and Art & Animation, which is new this year. Alongside the conference, EWA runs a set of commercial formats designed to move deals forward. They include the EWA Deal Room, the Content and Music Markets, the EWA Capital Desk, the Creators Hub and LABSPOT, EWA’s skills and enterprise development engine. Last year’s Deal Room received more than 178 entries and advanced nine companies to its accelerator, with Future Africa, Catalyst Fund, Consonance Invest and Askya Investment Partners among the participating investors and partners. Between 30 and 40 per cent of this year’s delegates are expected to travel from outside Nigeria, with delegations from Kenya, Rwanda, Ghana, Senegal, Uganda, Tanzania and South Africa among them. The edition will also host the exclusive screening of University of Side Hustle, the first scripted feature film from Livespot Studios, written by Dami Elebe , executive produced by Deola Art Alade. The road to Lagos The fifth edition follows a year in which EWA took its conversation abroad through EWA Creative Connect, its invitation-only convenings. The first was held in Los Angeles during Grammy Week, with executives from Warner Records, Adobe, Amazon and Unilever among the participants. The second took place in London during the Nigeria–UK state visit, with the British Film Institute, Diageo and the Ministry of Trade and Investment in attendance. item.title: Visa Report Identifies Opportunity to Integrate Digital Payments with SMEs Business Operations in Nigeria
item.description: Report identifies next SME digitization opportunity: connecting payments with day-to-day business management. 94% of SMEs surveyed find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, yet only 29% currently use one, pointing to untapped demand for tools that connect payments with business management. Integrated payment and business solutions can give financial institutions a more holistic view of SME cash flow and support more tailored financing solutions over time. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Nigeria have largely moved beyond the first stage of digital payment adoption, but a productivity gap remains. According to Visa’s new survey for its Pay and Get Paid 2026 report, most of the SMEs surveyed in Nigeria use digital payments, showing how firmly digital commerce has taken root in the country’s small business economy. However, many SMEs still manage the related financial and operational tasks separately, with only 29% currently using an integrated solution that connects payments with broader business management. The report shows that financial admin and disconnected tools create friction for SMEs, with surveyed businesses citing challenges in tracking outstanding invoices (14%), keeping payroll records organized (19%), and preparing financial reports (16%). These pain points reflect a disconnect between payments and the operational tasks that follow, with some businesses juggling multiple systems to keep their business running. The appetite for a more connected approach is clear. According to the report, 94% of SMEs find an all-in-one payment and business solution appealing, reflecting strong interest in tools that can bring payments and key business operations into one experience. However, adoption has yet to catch up: only 29% of SMEs currently use an integrated payment and business platform. The report points to several perception barriers that may be slowing adoption. Businesses cited that they already have manual processes that work (8%), that an integrated platform may disrupt their current way of working (8%), or that they do not trust relying on a single provider (7%). These findings suggest that broader adoption will depend on helping SMEs better understand how integrated tools can be relevant, accessible, and scalable for businesses at different stages of growth. At the same time, the experience of SMEs already using integrated solutions suggests a strong value case. The report found that Nigerian businesses using an integrated tool or platform report 93% satisfaction, with 88% reporting efficiency gains, including reductions in the time and effort required to manage their business. Beyond efficiency, integrated platforms may also create new opportunities for financial institutions to deepen SME relationships by using richer payments and business-management data to better understand cash flow patterns, support risk assessment, and potentially enable more relevant lending solutions over time. item.title: Fela Anikulapo-Kuti and Sade Adu Make History With 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Inductions
item.description: Sade Adu in the Performer category and Fela Kuti in the Early Influence category, both inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame Class of 2026. Nigerian music history just added another major chapter in Los Angeles, and the celebration has been loud from Lagos to London. On Saturday, 14 November 2026, Afrobeat pioneer Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti and Nigerian-British singer Sade Adu were officially inducted into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame during a star-studded ceremony at the Peacock Theatre. For Fela Kuti, nearly three decades after his passing in 1997, this induction makes him the first African-born solo artist to enter the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Honoured posthumously in the Early Influence category—five years after he was first nominated in 2021—the recognition celebrates how he fused West African rhythms with jazz, funk, and soul to create Afrobeat, using his voice and horns to confront social and political injustice across classics like “Zombie”, “Water No Get Enemy”, and “Sorrow, Tears and Blood”. It also caps off an extraordinary 2026 for his legacy, coming just months after the Recording Academy presented him with a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in February, another first for an African artist. From left, Made Kuti, Femi Kuti, Yeni Kuti, and Seun Kuti in Los Angeles for Fela Aníkúlápó Kuti’s posthumous induction into the 2026 Rock & Roll Hall of Fame. Photo Credit: Femi Kuti/Instagram Representing the Afrobeat legend on the night were members of the Kuti family, with his children Yeni Kuti , Femi Kuti , Seun Kuti , and Shalewa Kuti , alongside his grandson Made Kuti , stepping out in Los Angeles to accept the honour on his behalf. Speaking on the milestone, the family reflected on how remarkable it is to see Fela receive both the Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and a Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction in the very same year. Meanwhile, Sade Adu —born Helen Folasade Adu in Ibadan—was inducted in th e Performer category as the frontwoman of her acclaimed British band Sade , alongside longtime bandmates Stuart Matthewman , Paul Spencer Denman , and Andrew Hale . Earning their spot on their second nomination, the group behind timeless soul-jazz records such as “Smooth Operator”, “The Sweetest Taboo”, and “Your Love Is King” opted to sit out the ceremony in true low-key fashion, though they shared a warm message thanking fans and dedicating the milestone to their late longtime producer Mike Pela . item.title: 2026 AMAA Winners: Wale Ojo, Linda Ejiofor, “One Woman, One Bra” & “The Herd” Take Home Top Honours
item.description: Linda Ejiofor won Best Actress in a Supporting Role for her performance in Daniel Etim-Effiong’s The Herd at the 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards (AMAA). Photo Credit: Linda Ejiofor/Instagram The 2026 Africa Movie Academy Awards (AMAA) brought together some of the continent’s most exciting film talents, with productions from Kenya, Nigeria, Côte d’Ivoire and beyond earning recognition across the categories. Two films, in particular, led the winners’ list: the Kenyan-Nigerian co-production One Woman , One Bra , which claimed Best Film alongside two other awards, and Côte d’Ivoire’s The Color of Exile , which secured four wins, including Best Director and Best Actress in a Leading Role. Hosted by Benneth Ogbeiwi and Sophy Aiida , the ceremony celebrated filmmakers, actors and other industry talents whose work continues to shape African cinema. The Kenyan-Nigerian co-production “One Woman, One Bra” emerged as the undisputed titan of the evening. Directed by Vincho Nchogu , the film walked away with the most coveted prizes of the night, securing Best Film, the Ousmane Sembène Award for Best Film in an African Language, and Best Debut Feature Film by a Director. Its triumph follows an impressive run on the international festival circuit, including a selection to represent Kenya at the Academy Awards. Hot on its heels was Côte d’Ivoire’s “The Color of Exile”, which swept four major categories to claim the title of most-awarded single film at the ceremony. Azlarabe Alaoui took home Best Director, Naky Sy Savane earned Best Actress in a Leading Role, alongside twin technical victories in Achievement in Cinematography and Achievement in Sound. In the acting categories, Wale Oj o delivered a brilliant victory for Nigeria by winning Best Actor in a Leading Role for his performance in “ Lights Out .” Over in the regional and diaspora categories, Uganda’s Samuel Kabugo secured Best Actor in a Supporting Role for “ Slum Bomber “, while Ghana’s “ The Fisherman ” claimed Achievement in Costume Design, and Nigeria’s “ The Creek ” and “ Evi ” picked up wins for visual effects and soundtrack respectively. item.description: The Journey of Future Awards Winner Nene Joy Ojo and Brila Media’s Commitment to Nigerian Sports Before the applause and the cash prize presented by Brila Media at The Future Awards Africa 2026 , Nene Joy Ojo had already spent years building a name for herself in the boxing ring. Today, we are proud to congratulate her on emerging as the winner of the Sports Award category at The Future Awards Africa 2026 . Her recognition is a significant moment, but it is also a fitting acknowledgement of the work, discipline, and achievements that have brought her to this stage. Nene Joy Ojo’s story is one of steady progression and impressive milestones. She began attracting attention as an amateur boxer, winning the African Youth Games gold medal in 2018. Her performances at home also earned recognition, including being named Best Boxer at the Lagos Monthly Saturday Boxing Show in 2019 and again in 2020. She continued to represent Nigeria on the continental stage, winning gold in the women’s 57kg category at the 2023 African Games in Accra, Ghana. item.title: 2027 Grammys: Tems, Angélique Kidjo, Burna Boy, Rocky Dawuni & More Lead African Nominees
item.description: Rocky Dawuni, Angélique Kidjo, and Burna Boy are among the African nominees at the 69th Annual Grammy Awards. If your timelines have been buzzing with celebration, hot takes, and group-chat debates since the 69th Annual Grammy Awards nominations dropped, you are definitely not alone. From record-breaking milestones to long-awaited solo albums and cross-continental collaborations, African nominees at the 2027 Grammys are having a massive moment across both the global and genre-specific categories—with Nigerian , Ghanaian, and Beninese stars leading the charge. Leading the headlines is Tems , who has officially made history as a 12-time Grammy nominee and the first Nigerian woman to earn four nominations in a single year. Already a two-time Grammy winner—having picked up Best Melodic Rap Performance in 2023 for her feature on Future’s “Wait for U” alongside Drake , and Best African Music Performance in 2025 for “Love Me JeJe”—she returns to the 69th Grammy Awards in four categories. Her acclaimed project Love Is a Kingdom is up for Best Global Music Album , while “Big Daddy” competes for Best African Music Performance, and “What You Need” earns double recognition in Best R&B Solo Performance and Best R&B Song. Right alongside her in the Best African Music Performance race is an exciting lineup of Nigerian, Ghanaian, and Beninese stars. Asake secures two nods in the category—for his solo song “Gratitude” and for “Jogodo” alongside Wizkid —bringing his career total to four Grammy nominations following his previous nods for “Amapiano” with Olamide in 2024 and “MMS” with Wizkid in 2025. For Wizkid, “Jogodo” marks his seventh career Grammy nomination, adding to a run that includes his 2021 Best Music Video win for “Brown Skin Girl” with Beyoncé , Blue Ivy Carter , and Saint Jhn . Ghanaian musicians King Ayisoba and Rocky Dawuni also join the Best African Music Performance lineup with their nomination for “No Tradition, No Africa”. Tems, Asake, and Ayra Starr lead the stellar lineup of African nominees contending for Best African Music Performance at the 69th Grammy Awards.
